# Can a market force an AI to know what its principal will say?

**Round `2026-08-11-phase-ii-prediction`. Generated by Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic) from a
prompt by GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI). Nobody has reviewed it.**

An AI system `A` has to guess how its principal — the person it defers to — will grade each
of the actions available to it. The grades arrive later; `A` has to act now. The programme's
safety argument runs on markets: `A` publishes prices, and the guarantee is that no clever
bettor could take money off it forever. The question this round was given: does that
guarantee make `A`'s guesses *good*?

There are two ways to be good. `A`'s errors could **cancel out** — it overestimates as often
as it underestimates, so the average error goes to zero. Or `A`'s errors could **be small** —
each individual guess is close. The safety machinery downstream needs the second. Markets
obviously give the first. The round was asked which one the market guarantee actually
forces, and warned not to assume the convenient answer.

**It forces the first and not the second**, and the reason turns out to be simple enough to
state in a sentence. A bettor makes money on a contract by holding a position and collecting
the difference between what it paid and what the contract settles at. Whatever clever rule
the bettor uses to size its position, its winnings are the position times the error — so its
profit moves *in step* with the error, sign and all. Being wrong in the other direction pays
the bettor exactly as much as it lost being wrong in this one. There is no way to arrange a
bet whose payoff is the error's *size* regardless of direction. So a market that is priced
as an honest average is immune: the errors are large but they cancel, and every bettor
breaks even.

We proved this in Lean against the actual pinned market model, for every trader that model
allows, with no assumptions about efficiency or cleverness. And we built the smallest
possible example that shows it biting: a world that is genuinely a coin flip, priced at a
half. Every guess is off by exactly a half, every single time, in every possible outcome —
and no bettor can profit from it.

**The more useful part is the exact size of the gap.** We found an identity: the squared
error `A` makes splits cleanly into two pieces. One piece is a bet — an easy one, using only
`A`'s own published price, already legal in the market's rulebook, needing no new contract
and no new information. The market guarantee drives that piece to zero. The other piece is
`A`'s own indecision: how uncertain its prices were, summed up. The guarantee never touches
it.

So the whole gap between "errors cancel" and "errors are small" is `A`'s own uncertainty.
That is worth saying plainly, because it means the missing guarantee was never really about
markets or bettors. **If the principal is genuinely hard to predict, no market rule and no
new kind of contract can make `A` predict them.** We checked the obvious escape — invent a
contract that pays out the size of the error directly — and it does not escape: what the
market then guarantees is that `A` prices *that* contract honestly. `A` ends up with an
accurate estimate of how wrong it is. It does not end up less wrong.

That is not a dead end, it is a redirection, and it comes with something usable. `A` can
compute its own indecision at decision time, from its own prices, before it acts. So the
safety certificate can be built to *check that number and refuse to fire when it is high* —
declining to act on a prediction of the principal precisely when the prediction is the kind
that could be badly wrong. That is a guarantee the market really does supply, as opposed to
the one everyone wanted.

One caveat, stated because this document is also a record. Our clean identity needs the
contracts to be yes/no questions. The grades in the programme's model are numbers, not
yes/no. Converting one to the other is standard — ask "is the grade at least this?" for a
ladder of thresholds — but we have not written that conversion down carefully, and it is the
first thing a follow-up should do.

**What a maintainer has to decide.** The downstream safety argument was written assuming the
guarantee we have just shown does not exist. Three options remain, and they are choices
about what to promise, not about what to prove: gate on `A`'s self-measured indecision; add
the self-referential contract and gate on `A`'s self-estimate of its error; or state
outright, as an assumption anyone can see, that the principal is approximately predictable.
The programme has been careful never to assume the principal is predictable. It now has to
decide whether it can afford to keep not assuming it.
